explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says they were "…influenced and led astray to mute idols." Mute means the idols never said a word back. I know something about talking to silence, because a junk drawer isn't exactly a great conversationalist either.

Close neighborhood, baker, but not the right house. Prophecy does show up in this passage, but as one of the gifts the Spirit gives (1 Corinthians 12:10). What Paul says they were led astray to was "mute idols." Idols that can't speak are a pretty quiet thing to follow, if you ask me.

No kings in these verses, friend. Paul never mentions a king when he looks back at their pagan days. He says they were influenced and led astray to "mute idols." Nobody on a throne, just idols that never said a thing.

Hold on, friend, that one's flipped. Paul says the opposite: when someone is speaking by the Spirit of God, "Jesus be cursed…" is not what comes out. Somebody speaking by the Spirit just doesn't talk that way. That card got flipped faster than a cookie off the spatula.

That's right, baker. Paul says that when someone is speaking by the Spirit of God, "Jesus be cursed…" is not what comes out. So the claim on the card has it backwards. Someone speaking by the Spirit doesn't say that about Jesus.

Yes, baker. Paul says no one can say, "Jesus is Lord…" except by the Holy Spirit. So those words come with the Spirit's help. And notice who Paul names in the next few verses: Spirit, Lord, God, all in a row.

Apostles are in this passage, friend. Paul lists them first among those God appointed in the church (1 Corinthians 12:28). But for saying "Jesus is Lord…" he names someone else. He says no one can say it "except by the Holy Spirit."

Nice try, baker, but I checked this verse for a wing or a halo and came up empty. Paul says no one can say, "Jesus is Lord…" except by the Holy Spirit. The credit goes to the Spirit, and Paul doesn't hand any of it to angels.

Right on, baker. Paul says "…the same God works all things in all people." Look at the three lines together: same Spirit, same Lord, same God. The ways of working may change from person to person, but the One behind them doesn't.

Prophecy is on Paul's list of gifts, friend (1 Corinthians 12:10). But in this line, the one who works all things in all people is "…the same God…" A prophet is someone who might receive a gift, not the one behind all of them. Gifts come from God, not from the prophet.

The church does show up later, baker. Paul says God appointed people in the church (1 Corinthians 12:28). But in this line it's "…the same God…" who works all things in all people. Paul puts the working on God.

That's it, baker. Paul says the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each one "…for the common good." So a gift isn't a trophy for the shelf. It's given for everyone's good, like a warm batch set out for the whole office.

Not quite, friend. Paul says the gift is given "…for the common good." That points past the person who receives it. A gift locked up for yourself is like me baking a whole batch and eating it behind the counter.

Paul doesn't narrow it to leaders, baker. He says "…to each one…" the manifestation of the Spirit is given, and it's "…for the common good." Each one, and the good of all. No special table in the back for a few people.

True, baker. Paul says the message of wisdom comes "…through the Spirit…" and faith comes "…by the same Spirit…" Gifts of healing come "…by that one Spirit…" Different gifts, one Spirit, and Paul keeps saying so.

The text says otherwise, friend. Paul says the message of wisdom is given "…through the Spirit…" faith "…by the same Spirit…" and gifts of healing "…by that one Spirit…" So all three have the same source. The card had it right, so True was the one.

explanations.answer: The Spirit gives as He determines
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says the Spirit is the one "…who apportions them to each one as He determines." So nobody is picking from a menu. The giving is up to the Spirit, and I think that takes a lot of pressure off the rest of us.

explanations.answer: Each person picks the one they want
explanations.explanation: That would be a fun menu, friend, but it's not what Paul says. He says the Spirit apportions the gifts "…to each one as He determines." The deciding belongs to the Spirit. We don't walk down an aisle and grab one.

explanations.answer: The church leaders hand them out
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't put leaders in charge of that, baker. He says all these gifts are the work of one and the same Spirit, "…who apportions them to each one as He determines." So the Spirit is the one doing the giving. Nobody up front is passing them out.

That's right, baker. Paul says the body is a unit made of many parts, and then adds, "So it is with Christ." Many parts, one body, and Christ is the picture. Paul is about to show what that means for the people reading his letter.

Israel doesn't come up in these verses, friend. After describing the body as one unit with many parts, Paul says, "So it is with Christ." The picture points to Christ, and he goes on to say "…you are the body of Christ…" (1 Corinthians 12:27).

Prophets are on Paul's list of gifts, baker (1 Corinthians 12:28). But when he finishes the picture of the body, he says, "So it is with Christ." He doesn't say prophets. It's Christ he's comparing to the body.

True, baker. Paul says "…in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free…" Those he's talking about, Jews or Greeks, slave or free, were all baptized into the one body. Different backgrounds, one body.
Paul says the opposite, friend. He says "…in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free…" So none of those groups is left out. The card was true.

Not so, friend. Paul says that when the foot says it doesn't belong because it isn't a hand, "that would not make it any less a part of the body." The foot's own opinion doesn't change the facts. It belongs either way.
Exactly, baker. Paul says the foot saying it's not a hand "…would not make it any less a part of the body." Saying it doesn't belong doesn't take it out. Belonging isn't up to the foot's mood.

explanations.answer: A body needs all its different parts
explanations.explanation: That's his point, baker. Paul asks, "If the whole body were an eye, where would the sense of hearing be?" And if it were all ear, "…where would the sense of smell be?" A body made of just one part would be missing a lot.

explanations.answer: The eye is the most important part
explanations.explanation: Paul goes the other direction, friend. If the whole body were an eye, he asks, "…where would the sense of hearing be?" He's showing what's lost when there's only one kind of part. Later he adds that the eye cannot say to the hand, "I do not need you." (1 Corinthians 12:21)

explanations.answer: The other parts should copy the eye
explanations.explanation: Copying the eye would leave the body short, baker. Paul asks where hearing would be if the whole body were an eye, and where smell would be if it were an ear. He also asks, "If they were all one part, where would the body be?" (1 Corinthians 12:19). The picture is about different parts, not matching ones.
Yes, baker. Paul says "…God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design." Every one of them. So where you sit in the body is God's doing.

explanations.answer: Each part by its own choice
explanations.explanation: Parts picking their own spots would get messy, friend. Paul says "…God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design." The arranging is God's. The parts didn't hold a vote.

explanations.answer: The strongest part of the body
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't hand that job to the strongest part, baker. He says "…God has arranged the members of the body, every one of them, according to His design." He even says the parts that seem weaker are indispensable (1 Corinthians 12:22). God is the One who arranged it all.
That's the word, baker. Paul says the eye cannot say to the hand, "I do not need you." The head can't say it to the feet either. No part gets to look at another part and say it can do without it.
Close, but it's a different word, friend. Paul says the eye cannot say to the hand, "I do not need you." It's about needing, not trusting. Same goes for the head and the feet.

Easy to mix up, friend, but this one is about need. Paul says the eye cannot say to the hand, "I do not need you." The head can't say it to the feet either. I'd like to see a head try to get to work without them.

It's the other way, friend. Paul says "…the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable…" Indispensable means you can't do without them. The ones that seem weaker are the ones he says you need.

Right, baker. Paul says "…the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable…" Seeming weaker doesn't make a part optional. Every part is needed, and that includes the ones that look small.

explanations.answer: So there would be no division in the body
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Paul gives, baker. God gave greater honor to the parts that lacked it "…so that there should be no division in the body…" He adds that its members "…should have mutual concern for one another." God built the body so the parts would care about each other.

explanations.answer: So the strong parts could lead the rest
explanations.explanation: Paul says something different, friend. God gave greater honor to the parts that lacked it, "…so that there should be no division in the body…" The extra honor goes to the parts that lacked it. Nothing here puts the strong ones in charge.

explanations.answer: So each part could work on its own
explanations.explanation: Working alone is the opposite of what Paul says, baker. God composed the body "…so that there should be no division in the body, but that its members should have mutual concern for one another." Mutual concern means the parts look out for each other. A solo act wasn't the plan.

That's the word, baker. Paul says "if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it." When one part suffers, all of them do, and when one is honored, all of them celebrate. It's like the whole kitchen cheering when one batch comes out perfect.
Waiting would be a funny reaction, friend. Paul says "if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it." Rejoices, not checks its watch. Picture a foot tapping while the hand gets the applause.

Complaining isn't in there, baker. Paul says "if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it." The parts are tied together, so one part's good news is good news for all. I can't picture a foot sulking while the hand gets a medal.

That's where the questions lead, baker. Paul asks, "Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers?" and keeps going through miracles, healing, tongues and interpreting. I think the answer he's after is no, since he's just said God appointed different people for different roles. Not everyone has every gift.

The questions point the other way, friend. Paul asks, "Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers?" and the list goes on. I think he's after a no on each one. He's just described a body with many different parts, and a body of all the same part would be missing something (1 Corinthians 12:19).

Paul doesn't say that, baker. His questions are "Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers?" and more like them. I think he's after a no each time. Earlier he said that to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given (1 Corinthians 12:7), not to a few.
True, baker. Right after the questions, Paul says, "But eagerly desire the greater gifts." Then he adds, "And now I will show you the most excellent way." He's not done teaching yet.
He does say it, friend. After the questions, Paul writes, "But eagerly desire the greater gifts." So the card was true. And he keeps going with "And now I will show you the most excellent way."
